items.prompt: What is a usability test?

options.label: Comparing two designs by showing each to half of all live visitors
Asking a large sample to rate how much they like a product on a scale
Checking that a product's code runs without errors under heavy traffic
Watching people attempt realistic tasks to find where they struggle

rubric: A usability test observes task attempts to reveal problems.
Distractors describe surveys, load testing and A/B testing.

items.prompt: Which of these is an open-ended interview question?

options.label: Do you usually enjoy shopping online for your groceries?
Tell me about the last time you ordered groceries online.
Is price the most important factor when you order groceries?
Would you pay for a delivery subscription if it were offered?

rubric: Open-ended questions invite stories rather than yes/no answers.
The other options are closed or leading and invite short answers.

items.prompt: In participant recruitment, what is a screener?

options.label: A script the moderator reads aloud at the start of each session to explain the study
A tool that records the participant's screen and voice during a usability test
A report that summarises the main findings of a study for stakeholders
A short set of questions that checks whether someone fits the target participants

rubric: A screener filters candidates against criteria.
Distractors confuse it with a report, a script or a recording tool.

items.prompt: Which method most typically produces quantitative data?

options.label: One-on-one interview with open questions
Diary study with written notes
Survey with rating scales
Contextual observation in the field

rubric: Surveys with many respondents give numeric data that can be counted.
The others mainly produce qualitative data.

items.prompt: What does the 'think-aloud' technique ask participants to do?

options.label: Rate each screen from 1 to 10 once the session is done
Wait until the moderator asks before they say anything
Summarise the product's purpose before they start any task
Say their thoughts out loud while they work on tasks

rubric: Think-aloud means narrating thoughts during the task.
Other options describe ratings, summaries or silence.

items.prompt: Which of the following are common user research methods? Select all that apply.

options.label: Moderated usability testing
Load testing the servers
Surveys
Customer interviews
Code review

rubric: Usability tests, interviews and surveys study users directly.
Load testing and code review are engineering practices.

items.prompt: A researcher is about to begin a one-hour interview with a new participant. The participant has just joined the video call and the recording tool is ready. What should the researcher do first, before asking any research questions?

options.label: Start recording right away and ask the first warm-up question to save time
Show the participant the new design so they can react to it straight away
Ask the participant to describe everything they want the product to do next
Explain the study's purpose and get consent to take part and be recorded

rubric: Informed consent comes before data collection.
Other options skip consent or jump into content.

items.prompt: Why do researchers ask 'Tell me about the last time you did X' instead of 'Would you use a feature that does X?'

options.label: Participants are usually unwilling to answer questions about things that have not happened yet
Answers about hypothetical features are harder to code and compare across participants later
Past behaviour is a more reliable guide than people's predictions about themselves
Stories about past events tend to be longer and more detailed than answers about the future

rubric: People are poor at predicting their future behaviour.
Distractors give unrelated or overstated reasons.

items.prompt: In a usability test, 7 of 8 participants missed the Save button. How is this best classified?

options.label: A personal opinion about the visual style of the page
A market-size estimate for the product's potential audience
A statistically proven result about the whole user population
A usability problem found through observation of behaviour

rubric: Missing the button is observed behaviour that signals a usability problem.
Eight participants cannot prove a population statistic.

items.prompt: Why do many teams run usability tests with about five participants per round?

options.label: Most major problems show up early, so small rounds with fixes between them work well
Five participants give enough statistical power to generalise findings to the full user population
Five is the smallest sample for which task completion rates can be calculated reliably
Testing more than five at once makes moderators miss problems because sessions overlap

rubric: Small iterative rounds uncover recurring major issues efficiently.
Distractors wrongly claim statistical representativeness or rules.

items.prompt: Why is the question 'How much do you love our new search feature?' a poor interview question?

options.label: It is a closed question that forces the participant to answer with a number
It is too short and vague to prompt a detailed, useful answer
It assumes a positive opinion and pushes the participant toward it
It asks about a feature the participant may not have used yet

rubric: Leading questions bias answers toward the assumed view.
Other options misdiagnose the problem as length or format.

items.prompt: A team tests its new app only with colleagues from the same company. What is the most likely result?

options.label: Findings will be unusable because colleagues refuse to give feedback
Findings reflect insiders' knowledge and may miss problems real users face
Findings will match those of real users since the sessions are the same
Findings will be more accurate because colleagues know the product well and can speak for real users

rubric: Insiders differ from real users, so sampling bias hides problems.
Distractors assume familiarity helps or that the sample doesn't matter.

items.prompt: Which of these can make survey results misleading? Select all that apply.

options.label: Using a clear and consistent rating scale
Asking a question that mixes two topics at once
Keeping the survey short and focused
Leading or loaded question wording
Respondents who chose themselves to answer

rubric: Leading wording, self-selection and double-barreled questions distort results.
Clear scales and short surveys improve quality.

items.prompt: In an interview, a participant says, 'I'd definitely pay for a budgeting app like this.' Later they admit they have never used any budgeting tool, including free ones. How should the researcher interpret the first statement?

options.label: As weak evidence, since stated intent often differs from behaviour
As proof the participant is unsuitable and their other answers should be discarded
As a sign the interviewer should repeat the question until the answer is more reliable
As strong proof of demand, since the participant said 'definitely' with confidence

rubric: Stated intentions are weaker evidence than past behaviour.
Distractors overvalue the quote or blame the participant or method.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the difference between behavioral and attitudinal user research?

options.label: Behavioral research observes what people actually do, while attitudinal research collects what they say or feel
Behavioral research asks people about their goals, while attitudinal research counts clicks on a live product
Behavioral research is always quantitative, while attitudinal research is always done in person with a moderator
Behavioral research studies new users only, while attitudinal research studies long-term loyal customers only

rubric: Behavioral methods capture actions; attitudinal methods capture opinions and feelings.
Distractors confuse the split with quantitative vs qualitative or with user segments.

items.prompt: In a discovery interview, why is "Tell me about the last time you booked a trip" better than "Would you use an app that books trips for you?"

options.label: It lets the interviewer finish faster because the answers are shorter and easier to count
It shows the participant the product idea, so they can react to it in a more realistic way
It avoids open-ended answers, which are hard to compare across different participants
Past behavior is a more reliable guide than predictions about hypothetical future use

rubric: People are poor at predicting their own future behavior; real past events give grounded evidence.
Distractors mistake closed, quick answers for better data.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of a moderated usability test?

options.label: To estimate what share of the whole customer base will buy the product next year
To observe whether people can complete realistic tasks and see where they struggle
To learn which of two visual designs most participants say they like better overall
To collect feature requests directly from participants and rank them by popularity

rubric: Usability tests focus on task success and friction points.
Distractors describe preference polls, market sizing, or feature voting, which are other methods.

items.prompt: Which interview question is a leading question?

options.label: How did you decide which plan to choose?
Walk me through what you did after you added the item.
What, if anything, was confusing about checkout?
How much did you enjoy how easy our checkout was?

rubric: It assumes the checkout was easy and enjoyable, pushing the participant toward a positive answer.
The other options are neutral and open-ended.

items.prompt: Why do many practitioners run small usability tests with around five participants, then fix issues and test again?

options.label: Five is a rule set by industry standards bodies, so larger tests are not permitted
Five participants give statistically significant percentages that can be reported to stakeholders with confidence
Smaller samples remove the need for task scripts, since participants tend to behave in much the same way anyway
Each small round tends to reveal the most serious recurring problems, so they can be fixed before retesting

rubric: Usability testing is about finding problems; repeated small rounds surface major issues cheaply.
Distractors treat it as a statistical or mandated sample size.

items.prompt: Which of the following are primarily qualitative research methods? Select all that apply.

options.label: Contextual inquiry (observing users in their own environment)
Diary studies
Counting page views in analytics
One-on-one interviews
An A/B test measuring sign-up rates

rubric: Interviews, diary studies and contextual inquiry gather rich descriptions of experience.
A/B tests and page-view counts produce numeric, quantitative data.

items.prompt: A researcher interviews a participant who says, "I always use the search bar to find things." While watching the participant work on the site, the researcher sees them browse the menu every time and never touch search. What is the best interpretation?

options.label: Search must be broken, so the team should redesign it right away without running any more research first
Stated habits often differ from actual behavior, so the gap is worth probing and checking
Watching is less reliable than asking, so the participant's own statement should be treated as the final evidence
The participant is lying on purpose, so every one of their other answers should be discarded from the study

rubric: Self-reports often differ from behavior without any intent to deceive; treat the gap as something to explore.
Distractors jump to accusing the participant, assuming a cause, or trusting self-report over observation.

items.prompt: A team wants to know what share of its 2,000 customers used the export feature in the last month. Which method fits best?

options.label: A short survey or usage analytics covering the full customer base
A diary study with eight customers over two weeks
A card sort to group the export options into categories
Five moderated usability sessions with new users on the export screen

rubric: Estimating a share across many customers needs a quantitative method such as a survey or analytics.
Small qualitative methods cannot give a proportion.

items.prompt: A draft interview question reads: "Don't you find it frustrating when the app logs you out?" Which rewrite best fixes it?

options.label: Tell me about a time the app logged you out. What happened?
Is being logged out of the app frustrating, yes or no?
Wouldn't you agree that being logged out is a major problem?
How annoying is it when the app logs you out, from 1 to 5?

rubric: An open request for a real episode removes the leading framing and invites a story.
Other options still suggest frustration or force a narrow answer.

items.prompt: You are testing a food delivery app's reorder flow. Which task prompt is best for a usability test?

options.label: Tell us whether you like the reorder feature and how you might improve it.
Find the reorder feature and rate its design on a scale of 1 to 10.
You ordered a pizza last Friday and want the same meal tonight. Get it ordered.
Tap the 'Reorder' button on the order history screen and then press 'Confirm'.

rubric: A realistic goal-based task avoids naming interface labels, so it tests whether users can find the path.
Other options give away steps or ask for opinions rather than tasks.

items.prompt: After eight interviews you have pages of notes and sticky notes with quotes. What is the most appropriate next step to turn them into insights?

options.label: Pick the five most memorable quotes and send them to stakeholders as the findings
Count how many times each feature was mentioned and build whichever has the highest count
Rerun the same interviews with more participants until the notes stop varying
Group similar notes into themes (affinity mapping) and describe the patterns behind them

rubric: Affinity mapping synthesises observations into themes that support insights.
Distractors cherry-pick quotes, treat mentions as votes, or delay synthesis.

items.prompt: You are recruiting for a study of a budgeting app aimed at people who recently started managing their own money. Which screener criterion is best?

options.label: Is aged 18 to 65 and has used a banking app this month
Works in design or tech and knows UX research terms well
Says they love personal finance apps and enjoy trying new ones
Moved out or started a first paycheck job within the last year

rubric: Screening on a recent, specific behavior or situation finds the right participants.
Broad demographics, self-declared interest and industry insiders give weaker or biased samples.

items.prompt: You are about to moderate a usability test. Which actions should you take? Select all that apply.

options.label: Run a pilot session first to check the tasks and setup
Explain the design rationale if they criticise something
Tell them the session tests the product, not them
Ask the participant to think aloud while working
Give a hint as soon as they hesitate on a screen

rubric: Think-aloud, reassurance and piloting all support reliable, comfortable sessions.
Hinting or defending the design interferes with natural behavior.

items.prompt: In five usability sessions on a note-taking app, four participants could not find the 'Save draft' button and two abandoned the task. You must write the finding for the product team. Which version is best?

options.label: Users find the editor confusing overall, so the team should redesign the whole editor screen before release.
The 'Save draft' button is too small and the wrong colour, so make it larger and red to fix visibility.
Four of five participants could not find 'Save draft' and two quit; consider making it more visible and retest.
Participants seemed to prefer other note apps' layouts, so benchmark competitors in depth before changing anything.

rubric: A good finding states observed evidence with counts and ties a suggested direction to it.
Distractors overgeneralise, drift away from the evidence, or prescribe a fix without grounding.

items.prompt: Analytics show 45% of trial users abandon your app at step 3 of onboarding. The team needs to learn why people stall there. Which method should you run next?

options.label: Send an NPS survey to everyone who signed up this quarter
Run a card sort to test whether the onboarding step names make sense
Run moderated usability sessions of onboarding with target users
Launch an A/B test of a new button colour on step 3 to lift completion

rubric: Observing target users attempt onboarding reveals why they stall, which analytics can only locate.
NPS and A/B tests measure or compare but do not explain the cause; card sorting tests labels, not task flow.

items.prompt: You plan qualitative usability tests of a scheduling tool used by three very different groups: clinic receptionists, freelance coaches and school administrators. Their workflows barely overlap. How many participants should you plan for?

options.label: About 5 in total, picked at random from any group
1 per group, since the workflows are so different
About 5 per group, tested in small rounds
About 100 in total, so results are statistically significant

rubric: Small qualitative rounds uncover most problems within one homogeneous segment, so each distinct group needs its own sample.
Pooling 5 across groups misses segment-specific issues; 100 is for quantitative work, and 1 per group is too thin.

items.prompt: You are interviewing shoppers about how they find products on your site. Which opening question is the best-formed, non-leading choice?

options.label: Don't you find site search frustrating when results are off?
How much would you like a smarter search feature added?
Tell me about the last time you looked for a product here.
Would you say our search is easy to use or hard to use?

rubric: Asking about a specific past episode elicits real behaviour without suggesting an answer.
The other options lead the participant, force a closed judgement, or ask for hypothetical wishes.

items.prompt: You need survey data on how often people export reports from your tool. Which question is best worded to give usable, unbiased frequency data?

options.label: Do you often export reports from the tool, or only occasionally?
How frequently would you say you export reports, on a scale from 1 (never) to 10 (constantly)?
How satisfied are you with exporting reports, and how often do you usually do it?
In the past 30 days, how many times did you export a report? (0, 1-2, 3-5, 6+)

rubric: A bounded recent period with concrete ranges avoids vague wording and recall problems.
'Often' is subjective, the double-barrelled option mixes two ideas, and an arbitrary 1-10 scale has no clear meaning.

items.prompt: You want to recruit people who personally send invoices at small firms. Which screener question best qualifies them without revealing the target answer?

options.label: Which of these do you handle yourself at work? (invoicing, payroll, hiring, ordering)
About how many people work at your company, and what is your role there in the business?
Are you a small business owner who sends invoices to customers as part of your job?
Do you personally send invoices to customers at work, even if only occasionally or rarely?

rubric: A multi-item list hides the target so people cannot simply say what they think qualifies them.
Yes/no and descriptive questions make the right answer obvious, and company size alone doesn't show who does invoicing.

items.prompt: You are about to facilitate a moderated usability test of a checkout flow. Which facilitation practices should you apply? Select all that apply.

options.label: Defend the design when a participant criticises it
Write tasks as goals, such as 'buy a gift for under $30', without naming buttons
Ask 'Do you like this page?' after every screen
Briefly explain how the checkout works before they start
Ask the participant to think aloud while working

rubric: Think-aloud and goal-based tasks expose natural behaviour and reasoning without priming.
Pre-explaining, defending the design and constant opinion questions bias or interrupt the participant's behaviour.

items.prompt: A field-service company wants to improve its app for technicians who work in basements and vans with poor signal and constant interruptions. You have two weeks and a small budget. You must learn how the app really fits into their workday. Which approach should you use?

options.label: Shadow 5 or 6 technicians on real jobs, observing and asking questions in context
Email a survey to 500 technicians asking them to rate how useful each current feature is
Hold a focus group at head office with technicians and managers to discuss daily app use
Run unmoderated remote usability tests with technicians on their own devices after work hours

rubric: Contextual observation captures environmental constraints and workarounds that people rarely report.
Surveys, home-based tests and head-office focus groups remove the real context, so key conditions like signal and interruptions are lost.

items.prompt: In concept interviews, 9 of 10 participants said they would definitely use a meal-planning feature. After launch, under 5% of users tried it. What is the most likely flaw in the research?

options.label: Participants judged the idea without seeing the final visual design, so they could not react to how the feature would actually look
Ten participants were too few to show real interest, so the strong enthusiasm in the interviews cannot be trusted
Interviews capture only what people say, so they are unreliable for judging how people will behave later
Participants were asked to predict future use instead of describing what they currently do

rubric: Stated intent about hypothetical behaviour overstates real use; past behaviour is a stronger evidence base.
Sample size and visuals are not the core issue, and claiming interviews can't inform behaviour is overbroad.

items.prompt: A survey emailed to all customers reports 80% satisfaction. Only 6% responded, and the response data shows most respondents are weekly power users. What is the best analysis of the result?

options.label: The result is reliable because 80% is a strong majority, so the low response rate matters little
The result is invalid because a response rate under 10% makes any survey data useless
The result is representative because the survey was emailed to every customer on the list
Self-selection likely inflates satisfaction, so it can't represent all customers

rubric: Those who respond are skewed to engaged users, so the figure describes them rather than the whole base.
Sending to everyone doesn't fix who answers, and a low rate alone doesn't automatically make a survey useless.

items.prompt: In a usability test of an export feature, two of five participants located it only after the moderator asked, 'Have you looked in the top menu?' The report counts all five as successes. What is wrong with the analysis?

options.label: Success should be judged by completion time alone, so the hinted participants should be compared with the others on speed
Five participants is too few to support any success rate, so the results should be set aside until more are recruited
Moderator-assisted completions hide a findability problem and should be recorded as assisted or failed
Participants who needed a hint are outliers, so their sessions should be removed and the success rate recalculated

rubric: Success achieved after a hint doesn't show the interface works unaided; it masks the findability problem.
Dropping those participants discards the key evidence, and time alone doesn't settle success.

items.prompt: After interviews, a team sorted its notes into groups named after product areas: 'Search', 'Filters', 'Settings', 'Profile'. The groups yielded no surprising insights. What is the most likely analytical problem?

options.label: Product-area groups repeat the team's own framing and hide user goals
Too few notes were collected, so no patterns could emerge across participants
Sticky notes are a poor medium, so synthesis should be done in a spreadsheet
Notes should be grouped by participant first, so each person's story stays intact

rubric: Organising by feature repeats the team's own framing; regrouping by goals, tasks or frustrations surfaces needs.
Grouping per participant prevents cross-participant patterns, and the medium isn't the issue.

items.prompt: Analytics show a reporting feature is used heavily, yet in interviews most users call it painful and say they avoid it when possible. Which interpretation best reconciles the two sources?

options.label: The interviewees are probably unrepresentative outliers, so the heavy usage data should guide the roadmap
Analytics are unreliable here, so the interviews should be trusted and the usage numbers set aside
Heavy usage may reflect a lack of alternatives, so probe the workarounds and forced tasks
Interviews are unreliable because people misreport habits, so trust the analytics and ignore complaints

rubric: Usage shows what people do, not whether it's good; forced use is plausible, so investigate why.
Dismissing either source or the participants skips the chance to understand the gap.

items.prompt: A study plan to test a banking app's transfer flow uses five friends of the team, tasks that say 'tap the Transfer tab', and a short pilot session beforehand, with consent-based recording. Which elements weaken the validity of the findings? Select all that apply.

options.label: Running a pilot session first
Writing tasks that name the exact button to tap
Recruiting friends of the team
Recording sessions with participants' consent

rubric: Friends are a biased sample, and naming the button removes the findability challenge being tested.
Pilot sessions and consented recording are good practice, not validity threats.

items.prompt: After a checkout redesign, support tickets about checkout confusion rose 30%. A usability test on the new flow with 8 participants showed everyone completing checkout easily. You notice all 8 were first-time buyers, while most tickets come from returning customers. What is the best next analytical step?

options.label: Roll back the redesign now, because a 30% rise in tickets outweighs a small usability test
Run a larger test with more first-time buyers, since 8 participants is too few to trust the result
Test returning customers and compare with the old flow, since the sample missed the ticket segment
Treat the tickets as noise, because the usability test showed every participant finishing easily

rubric: The test sample doesn't cover the segment generating tickets; returning users may be tripped by changed habits.
Ignoring tickets, blind rollback or more of the same segment doesn't address the sample mismatch.

items.prompt: In interviews, 9 of 12 participants said they would use a weekly budgeting report. Analytics show only 6% of users open the existing monthly report. Which explanation best accounts for the gap?

options.label: Participants were deliberately lying to please the interviewer, so the interview data should be discarded entirely
The analytics are unreliable because a 6% open rate is too small a share of users to support any conclusion at all
Weekly reports are inherently more valuable than monthly ones, so the current open rate says nothing about real demand
Answers about hypothetical future use tend to overstate intent, while analytics show what people actually do in context

rubric: Stated intent about hypothetical use is a weak predictor of behaviour, so the contrast is expected.
Distractors either dismiss the behavioural data or assume deliberate deception rather than ordinary overclaiming.

items.prompt: A usability test with 5 participants found 4 failed to locate the 'Invite teammate' button. All five were recruited from the company's own beta power users. What does this detail most affect about interpreting the result?

options.label: The finding is invalid because five participants can never reveal a real usability problem in any kind of test
The failure rate probably understates the problem for typical new users, since power users already know the product's conventions
Nothing, because recruitment source matters for surveys but has no bearing on task-based usability test results
The finding overstates the problem, since power users are more critical of every interface than newcomers would be

rubric: Participants more experienced than the target users make a failure at all more telling, so the true rate is likely higher.
Distractors reject small samples outright or assume experts are harsher, ignoring familiarity effects.

items.prompt: A satisfaction survey emailed to 8,000 customers got 240 responses (3%), averaging 4.6 out of 5. The team concludes customers are very satisfied. Which analysis identifies the main weakness?

options.label: Email surveys cannot measure satisfaction at all, so only interviews could ever have produced a valid conclusion
People who chose to answer likely differ from the silent 97%, so the average may reflect enthusiasts rather than all customers
A 4.6 average is too high to be believable, so the scale must have been built incorrectly by the survey team
240 responses falls below the minimum needed to compute any average, so the figure has no statistical meaning at all

rubric: Low, self-selected response creates non-response bias that undermines generalising the average.
Distractors blame the scale, the raw count or the channel instead of who responded.

items.prompt: After interviews, a researcher groups sticky notes under headings such as 'Search', 'Cart' and 'Profile'. The team later complains the themes give no direction. What is the most likely flaw in the analysis?

options.label: Affinity mapping is unsuitable for interview data and should be replaced by a statistical cluster analysis
Themes should have been counted and ranked by frequency before any grouping under headings was attempted
Too few sticky notes were created, so each theme lacked enough supporting quotes to convince the wider team
Grouping by product area mirrors the interface and hides the goals, tensions and workarounds that cut across screens

rubric: Themes tied to UI structure restate the product instead of surfacing user needs.
Distractors treat the problem as volume, ranking or method choice rather than the basis for grouping.

items.prompt: In an interview about checkout, the researcher asks, 'How frustrating was the payment step?' Most participants describe it as frustrating. Which analysis of this result is most accurate?

options.label: The result is weak only because the sample is small; the wording of a question has little effect on what people say
The question presupposes frustration, so answers are shaped by its wording and don't show whether payment was truly a problem
The result is strong evidence, because agreement from most participants shows the problem is widespread across all users
The question is fine because asking directly about emotion is the best way to uncover problems in a specific step

rubric: A leading question builds the answer into the prompt, so agreement is not evidence.
Distractors treat agreement as validation or blame sample size instead of wording.

items.prompt: A moderator runs a usability test of a booking site. Which practices threaten the validity of the findings? Select all that apply.

options.label: Participants are recruited to match the site's real customer segments rather than being colleagues
Sessions are screen-recorded so the team can review where participants hesitated afterwards
Task wording says 'Click Manage Booking to change your date', naming the exact menu label
The moderator says 'Maybe try the top menu' to participants who are stuck, before they give up

rubric: Naming UI labels in tasks and hinting both remove the discovery the test is meant to observe.
Representative recruiting and recording are good practice, not threats.

items.prompt: Support tickets about the 'export report' feature tripled this quarter, yet analytics show export clicks are flat and only 2% of users use it. Three interviews with ticket authors show each exports once a month for a finance close and misses a deadline when it fails. What is the best analysis?

options.label: Three interviews are too few to interpret anything, so the team should wait for a large survey before reading the tickets
Ticket growth with flat usage means support is miscategorising requests, which should be fixed before any research continues
Low usage hides high stakes: a small segment depends on export at a critical moment, so frequency alone understates its importance
Flat usage proves the tickets are noise, so export should stay low priority until its click numbers begin to rise

rubric: Combining sources shows rare but high-consequence use, so click frequency misleads.
Distractors dismiss the qualitative evidence or assume a data-quality fault without support.

items.prompt: A team must choose between two labelings of a settings area within two days, with budget for about 30 remote participants. Criteria: compare findability quantitatively; explaining why is not required. Which method best fits?

options.label: A two-week diary study in which participants log every time they search for a setting in daily use
A focus group of 8 users discussing which labels they prefer, then adopting the group's favourite
Contextual interviews with 6 participants to explore in depth how they think about settings and their labels
Tree testing both structures with about 15 participants each and comparing task success and directness

rubric: Tree testing gives fast, comparable findability metrics for competing structures within the budget.
Distractors are too slow, qualitative or preference-based for the stated criteria.

items.prompt: A researcher plans a 20-question multiple-choice survey to discover unmet needs freelancers have around invoicing, a space the team knows little about. Judge the plan against the goal of discovering unknown needs.

options.label: Weak fit: preset answers can only confirm needs the team already imagines, so run exploratory interviews first
Weak fit only because 20 questions is too long; cutting it to 10 would make the survey suitable for discovery
Strong fit if the survey is piloted first, since piloting with a few freelancers shows whether the options cover their needs
Strong fit: closed questions give quantifiable data, which is the best way to discover unknown needs at scale

rubric: Discovery needs open-ended input; closed options constrain answers to the team's assumptions.
Distractors mistake quantification for discovery or assume length or piloting fix the issue.

items.prompt: A team tests a new checkout with screen reader users. Criteria: find barriers in the real assistive setup, understand why users get stuck, and use no more than 6 participants. Which design best meets them?

options.label: Moderated remote sessions on participants' own devices and assistive tech, with think-aloud and probing questions
A post-launch survey asking screen reader users to rate checkout ease on a scale from 1 to 5
An automated accessibility scan combined with sighted team members simulating a screen reader eyes closed
Unmoderated tasks on a lab-provided laptop with default screen reader settings, scored by completion time

rubric: Own setups plus moderation reveal real barriers and their causes with a small group.
Distractors lose the real setup, the explanation of causes, or actual user involvement.

items.prompt: A designer argues that because 'five users find 85% of problems', one round of 5 sessions is enough to sign off a redesign and report that 90% of users can complete signup. Which critique is best?

options.label: The claim is sound because five users find 85% of problems, so a 90% completion estimate follows directly
Five sessions can surface major problems, especially over iterations, but cannot support a population completion-rate claim
Five sessions are too few for any usability problem to be found reliably, so a test needs at least 30 participants before any finding is trusted
The estimate is fine if the five participants are chosen to look typical, since careful selection replaces a larger sample

rubric: Small samples are good for finding problems, not for estimating rates with any precision.
Distractors over-extend the 85% heuristic, reject small tests outright, or treat selection as a substitute for sample size.

items.prompt: A PM wants to skip interviews and run an A/B test on onboarding to learn why 40% of new users abandon at step 2. Judge this against the goal of understanding why.

options.label: An A/B test shows which variant performs better, not why users leave, so qualitative sessions should come first
A/B tests are the best fit because large samples reveal motivations more reliably than a handful of interviews can
A/B tests are acceptable only if run longer, since extra test duration eventually reveals the reasons for abandonment
Interviews are unnecessary because the 40% drop-off at step 2 already identifies the cause of the abandonment

rubric: Experiments measure outcomes of changes; explaining behaviour requires qualitative evidence.
Distractors confuse where users drop off, or sample size, with why they do.

items.prompt: A team wants to understand how nurses use a medication-tracking app across shifts. Which are sound reasons to prefer a diary study over one-off interviews? Select all that apply.

options.label: It removes the need to follow up with participants after the entries are collected
It gives statistically representative estimates of how many nurses face each problem
It captures behaviour and context as they occur over days, reducing reliance on participants' memory
It can reveal variation between shifts and recurring interruptions that a single conversation would miss

rubric: Diary studies capture in-the-moment, longitudinal behaviour and variation across shifts.
They use small samples and usually need follow-up, so they neither estimate prevalence nor replace debriefs.

items.prompt: A sales lead sends three enthusiastic customers to give feedback on a new pricing page, and the PM wants to ship Friday on that basis. The team has five days and can recruit through a panel. Criteria: reduce selection bias and stay within the deadline. Which response is best?

options.label: Ask the three customers to nominate peers from their own networks, since referrals widen the sample without extra recruiting cost
Delay launch a month to run a 1,000-person survey, since only very large samples can counter selection bias in feedback
Ship Friday, since customers chosen by sales know the product best and their enthusiasm is strong evidence of success
Run five moderated sessions with panel-recruited target users within two days, and keep the three customers as extra input

rubric: Independent recruiting addresses selection bias and fits the five-day window.
Distractors keep the biased sample, miss the deadline, or recruit through the same friendly network.

items.prompt: Six discovery interviews surface a sharp pain point. A survey of 2,000 users shows only 8% report it. The team must decide how to weigh the two findings. Which judgement is best supported?

options.label: Defer to the survey, because its far larger random sample makes the interview finding statistically invalid for roadmap planning decisions
Average the two into a medium priority, because each method deserves equal evidential weight when findings conflict on a question
Check whether interviewees are a distinct high-value segment the survey average hides, then weigh impact by segment
Defer to the interviews, because depth of insight outweighs breadth of sample when the research goal is early discovery work

rubric: The methods answer different questions; the 8% average may mask a concentrated, high-impact segment.
Distractors apply a blanket rule about sample size, depth or averaging instead of examining who was sampled.

items.prompt: A usability test plan has five participants complete tasks, then asks each 'Would you use this feature?' and reports the percentage who said yes as the adoption forecast. Which critique is most defensible?

options.label: Stated intent predicts behaviour poorly, so the plan should rely on observed task behaviour and evidence of unprompted use
Five participants is too few to run a usability test, so the plan should wait until at least thirty are recruited
The question is fine, but it should be asked before the tasks so that experience does not bias the answer
Percentages are acceptable if the participants are representative, so the plan only needs better recruitment criteria

rubric: Self-reported intent is a weak proxy for behaviour; observed behaviour is stronger evidence.
Distractors fix sample size or order, which miss the validity problem of treating intent as a forecast.

items.prompt: A team studies why people who tried their app did not adopt it. They plan to recruit only from the active customer list. Rank the threats to validity: which is most serious for this research question?

options.label: Eight participants is a small sample, which limits how confidently the team can quantify any theme found
Interviewers may ask a few leading questions, which can be reduced with a better guide and a pilot session
A single note-taker may record events selectively, which can be reduced by recording sessions with consent
Active customers are survivors, so the sample leaves out the people who abandoned the app

rubric: Sampling only survivors removes the population the question is about, which cannot be repaired afterwards.
Other distractors are real but fixable or do not invalidate the question itself.

items.prompt: Criteria: an early prototype with ambiguous flows, a need to learn why users hesitate, results in two weeks. Which method is the best trade-off?

options.label: Unmoderated remote tests with 100 users, because larger numbers reveal reasons behind hesitation more reliably
Moderated sessions, because live probing exposes the reasons behind hesitation in ambiguous flows
Click-tracking on the prototype with session replays, because behavioural logs explain the reasons for hesitation without bias
A large survey on the prototype screenshots, because rating scales capture hesitation with little effort

rubric: Probing the why in an unfinished, ambiguous prototype needs a moderator who can follow up.
Distractors favour scale or logs, which show what happens but not why.

items.prompt: After ten interviews a synthesis slide says: '7 of 10 asked for dark mode, so it is our top priority.' Which evaluation of this claim is best?

options.label: Mention frequency is not priority; check whether requests were prompted, the underlying need, and the impact on user goals
It is sound, because a 70% mention rate in qualitative work is a strong indicator of priority
It is unsound only because ten participants is too few, so the team should repeat it with thirty
It is unsound because feature requests from users should be ignored, and only observed behaviour should be used

rubric: Counting requests conflates frequency with importance and ignores prompting and the underlying need.
Distractors either accept the count or reject all stated requests wholesale.

items.prompt: A team debates a two-week diary study versus single interviews to understand how people manage irregular household expenses. Which reasons justify choosing the diary study? Select all that apply.

options.label: The team needs precise task-completion times for a specific interface
The team needs statistically significant estimates of how many users hold each habit
The team wants the cheapest and fastest method available for the quarter
Behaviour unfolds over time and in context, which one conversation would flatten
Events are infrequent and in-the-moment, so recall in an interview would be unreliable

rubric: Diary studies suit rare, contextual, longitudinal behaviour where memory is poor.
Significance, speed and timing measures point to surveys, quick interviews or usability tests instead.

items.prompt: A checkout redesign wins an A/B test with a 4% conversion lift. Support tickets about confusing charges rose 15%, and in moderated sessions several users completed purchase by guessing. The team must choose the next step. Which is best?

options.label: Hold full rollout and test comprehension, refunds and repeat purchase, since the lift may be bought with later cost
Dismiss the sessions as too few to count, because only the experiment gives statistically reliable evidence here
Revert at once, because any rise in support tickets proves the redesign is worse than the old checkout
Ship it now, because a significant conversion lift is the primary success metric and tickets are secondary noise

rubric: Conversion alone can hide confusion that costs refunds and trust; downstream measures settle it.
Distractors overweight one signal either way or dismiss qualitative evidence by sample size.

items.prompt: You must learn how nurses chart during a shift. Constraints: no audio recording, no interrupting patient care, three weeks, eight nurses. Which design meets every constraint?

options.label: Video recording of the ward to capture charting precisely, then coding the footage during the three weeks
Eight 60-minute interviews in a meeting room, with the nurses' managers taking notes to keep the sessions efficient
Silent shadowing across shifts with handwritten notes, plus a short end-of-shift debrief to check interpretations
A survey of all hospital staff with rating scales, which avoids any presence on the wards during care

rubric: Shadowing with notes observes real work without audio or interruption; debriefs verify meaning.
Distractors break a constraint (recording) or lose workflow context (room interviews, survey).

items.prompt: Design a screener for a study on how freelancers handle client invoices. Needs: a mix of experience levels, exclusion of professional research participants and people employed by invoicing tools. Which screener design fits?

options.label: Ask applicants to rate their invoicing expertise from 1 to 10, then take only the highest raters because they will give richer and more detailed insight
Recruit only from one active freelancer forum, because members self-identify as freelancers and are already motivated to join a study for a small incentive
Ask 'Are you a freelancer who invoices clients?' and accept everyone who answers yes, so that the sessions fill quickly and on schedule
Ask about recent invoicing behaviour with non-obvious options, set experience quotas, and exclude recent study participants and invoicing-tool staff

rubric: Behavioural, non-leading questions with quotas and explicit exclusions meet all stated needs.
Distractors use a transparent yes/no screen, self-rated expertise, or a single self-selected channel.

items.prompt: You will interview people about managing personal debt, a sensitive topic. Goals: elicit real past behaviour, avoid leading, keep participants comfortable. Which opening sequence is best?

options.label: 'Do you manage your debt well?' then 'What tools would you like us to build for managing it?' to gather ideas for the product team
'Why do people get into debt?' then 'Do you feel ashamed of your debt?' to surface the emotions behind it early in the session
'Tell me about your day-to-day money routine,' then 'Walk me through the last time a bill was hard to pay'
'How much debt do you have?' then 'Which lender do you use?' to establish the basic facts before any other discussion begins

rubric: Starting broad and moving to a specific recent episode elicits behaviour while the participant controls disclosure.
Distractors lead, ask for opinions or solutions, or open with intrusive facts.

items.prompt: Your insight: 'Users abandon sign-up because pricing is unclear.' You have one week and must design a check that could disprove it. Which plan fits?

options.label: Run a workshop where the team votes on whether the insight feels right and then records the consensus
Show pricing variants to new visitors and observe sign-up behaviour, with pre-set criteria stating what result would reject the insight
Interview five churned users, asking whether unclear pricing influenced them, and record how many agree with the statement
Survey existing customers about how clear pricing feels and treat an average above 4 out of 5 as confirmation

rubric: A falsifiable test with pre-stated rejection criteria and behavioural measures can disprove the insight.
Distractors ask leading questions, sample survivors, or rely on opinion.

items.prompt: A proposed research plan lists the method, twelve participants, a discussion guide, a schedule and a report format. A senior researcher says something essential is missing. What is it?

options.label: A larger sample size, since twelve participants cannot support any decision the team might need to make
A longer discussion guide, since more questions would reduce the chance that a theme is missed
A named decision the study informs and what findings would change it, so results are actionable
A statement that the findings will be presented to leadership, so that the work gains organisational visibility

rubric: Without a decision and change criteria, a plan produces findings that cannot guide anything.
Distractors add scale, volume or visibility without linking to a decision.

items.prompt: A study of onboarding runs in three countries with local moderators, and findings must be comparable across countries. Which plan elements are needed to meet this? Select all that apply.

options.label: A shared core discussion guide, with local wording checked by pilot sessions or back-translation
Each moderator choosing their own questions to follow local culture most freely
A common coding frame, with moderators calibrating on a sample of transcripts
Recruiting only English speakers in every country to simplify analysis
Reporting each country separately without any shared themes or structure

rubric: A shared guide with validated localisation and calibrated coding keeps data comparable.
Free-form questions, English-only samples, or separate reports undermine comparability or representativeness.

items.prompt: A founder wants to know whether small restaurants will pay for an inventory tool. There is no prototype, four weeks remain, and the evidence must show willingness to pay, not polite interest. Which plan best meets this?

options.label: Demo a slide concept to owners in one-hour sessions, then collect written feedback and enthusiasm ratings from each of them
Run a landing page with paid ad traffic for four weeks and judge demand by the number of email sign-ups it collects
Interview owners about current stock handling, then ask for a commitment such as a paid pilot or signed letter of intent
Send a survey to a few hundred owners asking whether they would pay for such a tool and what monthly price they would accept

rubric: Past-behaviour interviews plus a costly commitment test real willingness to pay without a prototype.
Distractors rely on hypothetical answers, enthusiasm or free sign-ups, which are cheap signals.
